Insinkerator Under-sink instant hot water heater

incident_description:
Following is my review of the Insinkerator SST instant hot water heater on the Walmart website, that explains the issue.  There were no injuries, but there is likely a potential for electric shock or  fire.  UPC number and manufacturing date are not shown on the product.  I can't remember where purchased--it was an on-line website.
"[Name Redacted], in his March 2020 review on the Walmart website, got it right:  the Insinkerator SST under-sink instant water heater has a design flaw, with the vinyl tube that is in contact with the hot water tank getting brittle and cracking, causing a water leak.  After reading the review, I opened up my ~5-year-old leaking SST unit and sure enough--the tube was exactly as described in the review:  discolored dark brown and had a hard scabby cracked area where it contacted the tank, that was the source of the leak (see photo).  The leak caused water to drip on the electrical components below the tank.  Any time that electrical components get wet, there is a presumed possibility of hazards such as shock and fire.  Not to mention water damage to kitchen cabinetry.
[Name Redacted] noted that he spliced a length of copper tube in place of the vinyl tube and has had several years of satisfactory leak-free service from his unit.  But it may not be a good idea to continue using any electrical device that has had its electrical components drenched in water.  I did some research, and it looks like vinyl tubing has a maximum temperature limit of around 140 to 160 degrees F, which makes it obvious that vinyl tubing is inappropriate for contact with a hot water tank at near-boiling water temperature (212 F).  The Insinkerator engineers couldn't figure this out?  Perhaps food-grade silicone tubing, with a temperature limit of over 400F, well above water boiling point, might be a better design choice."
expert_rationale: Incident identifies Insinkerator / SST, which conflicts with the recalled product scope Sump Pumps sold under Utilitech, Do It and Star Water Systems brands.

On 6/30/20 I had mowed our lawn and proceeded to pick up clippings with our lawn sweeper attached to our 2020

incident_description:
Re: UNREASONABLE RISK OF SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH CONCERNING
HONDA CRF250R MULTIPLE YEAR MODELS AND OTHER DISPLACEMENT
MOTOCROSS OFF-ROAD HONDA MOTORCYCLES AND DENSO STATORS
DUE TO ELECTRICAL FAILURE AND SUDDEN UNINTENDED ENGINE SHUT
OFF ENGINE FAILURE DURING OPERATION AND WHILE IN MOTION.

I. REPORT AND COMPLAINT SUBMITTED IN ORDER TO PROTECT
CONSUMERS AND OTHER RIDERS FROM FORESEEABLE FUTHER
INJURIES OR DEATH DUE TO KNOWN UNSAFE AND UNREASONABLY
DANGEROUS HONDA AND DENSO DEFECTIVE PRODUCTS.

This Report and Complaint is respectfully submitted to the United State Consumer
Product Safety Commission in order to prevent foreseeable further injuries and
potential deaths due to known defective products put into the stream of
commerce by Honda and Denso and sold to Americans countrywide and affecting
certain motorcycles worldwide.

II. AMERICAN HONDA MOTOR CO., INC., HONDA MOTOR CO., LTD., DENSO
CORPORATION AND THE HONDA CRF250R.
This Report and Complaint and attachment(s) concerns certain model years Honda
CRF250R motocross off-road motorcycles manufactured by Honda Motor Co., LTD in
Japan and sold in the United States by American Honda Motor Co., Inc., with stators
incorporated thereto manufactured by Denso Corporation.
The population of affected Honda off-road motocross motorcycles are unsafe and
unreasonably dangerous to operate and must now be investigated, recalled and
properly remedied.

III. SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES
UNLIMITED CIVIL CASE.

In re and subsequent to the [REDACTED] [settled favorably for the Plaintiff]), we present facts that uncontrovertibly
demonstrate the clear existence of product defects that make certain model year Honda
CRF250R motorcycles unsafe and unreasonably dangerous to operate resulting in
unreasonable risk of serious injury or death.

American Honda Motor Co., Inc., Honda Motor Co., LTD., and Denso Corporation have
known for years about the foregoing product defects but have failed to report or recall
their defective unreasonably dangerous products.

IV. SUDDEN UNINTENDED ENGINE SHUT OFF DUE TO PRODUCT DEFECT.

The product defects contained within the 2014 and many other year model Honda
CRF250Rs, because they can result in the motorcycle’s engine suddenly and
unexpectedly turning off during operation and ceasing operation in its entirety while in
motion (unintended engine shut off), which exposes children, retail end users and other
riders to unreasonable risk of serious injury or death because the motorcycle’s engine
can suddenly and unexpectedly stop running and operation without any indication it is
about to fail.

The failure of the engine to continue running when appropriate may cause loss of
control, leading to motorcycle crashes and therefore significantly raises the risk of
serious injury or death.

V. REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF HONDA AND DENSO; REQUEST FOR
INVESTIGATION AND RECALL OF UNREASONABLY DANGEROUS
PRODUCTS.

This Report and Complaint are submitted to formally request investigation of Honda and
Denso and recalls of the affected Honda CRF250R (and Honda CRF450R [and any
other model using similar Denso stators]) off-road motocross motorcycle populations in
the United States in order to reduce the unreasonable risk of serious injury or death to other unsuspecting operators. This Report and Complaint should be forwarded to your
counterparts in Canada and Europe wherein Honda has marketed and sold its defective
CRF250R off-road motocross motorcycles.

This Report and Complaint concerns a 2014 model year Honda CRF250R incident off road motocross motorcycle, a similar brand new 2014 model year Honda CRF250R
exemplar off-road motocross motorcycle, other similar models, and approximately five
or more years-worth of production Honda CRF250R motorcycles.

Multiple model years and multiple displacement off-road motorcycles are affected by the
product defect(s) and should be recalled by the manufacturer.

To our knowledge, Honda and Denso and their various business entities have not
voluntarily recalled these products.

Stator failures have occurred in the United States and Europe. Stator failures have
occurred with racing teams.

The manufacturer has subsequently improperly used or directed to be used, epoxy as a
means to secure defective stator wires. Honda likes gluing together important electrical
connections and Denso does not know whether their stators will be used on
motorcycles with or without 12VDC batteries and the results thereof. Both are
significant failures and embarrassments to Honda and Denso respectively.

The use of epoxy to additionally secure defective stator wires is below the standard of
care and not in accord with industry standards.

Honda and Denso have actual knowledge of the product defects that form the basis of
this Report and Complaint.

Honda and Denso should provide the Consumer Product Safety Commission with all
information, data and documents relevant to the matter in order to facilitate
determination of the scope of the defective stator’s utilization in the population of
motorcycles it has sold to the American public and worldwide. A thorough investigation
by the CPSC will likely uncover the defects are both manufacturing and design defects.

A recall of all affected Honda off-road motorcycles using defective Denso stators will
help ensure no children or adults are seriously injured or killed as a result of Honda’s
knowing and continued use of defective electrical components.
VI. HONDA STATOR FAILURES AND UNINTENDED ENGINE SHUT OFF
RESULTING IN ENGINE FAILURE AND SUBSEQUENT OPERATOR
PARALYSIS.

I was retained in order to look into a 2014 Honda CRF250R off-road motocross
motorcycle, its sudden unintended engine shut off and crash, operated by a licensed
professional rider, during practice, on a motorcycle closed-circuit dirt track.

The facts of the case indicate the incident 2014 Honda CRF250R’s engine suddenly
and unintentionally shut off during normal and foreseeable operation, resulting in a
horrendous crash and subsequent rider paralysis. An objectively tragic outcome directly
caused Honda’s defective product.

As part of the case workup, we determined a copper wire in the motorcycle’s stator
located within the engine of the incident motorcycle had failed, fractured and
disconnected. The stator is made by Denso for Honda is at issue concerning these
defective unreasonably dangerous off-road motocross motorcycles, please see infra.

If a stator copper wire fractures the result is the engine shuts off (extremely fast, no prior
warning) in under 4/10’s of a second. Stators are not generally considered wear items
and are expected to last the life of most motorcycles.

As general mechanical and operational propositions and industry standards, stator
wires do not just become disconnected absent something more. The stator is internal to
the motorcycle’s engine and it is not a component that can be damaged by merely
operating and riding these machines.

The crash of this 2014 Honda CRF250R off-road motocross motorcycle left the operator
seriously injured resulting in paralysis and he is now permanently handicapped in a
wheelchair for the rest of his life due to a particular defective Honda motorcycle.

As a court qualified motorcycle expert in the field of motorcycles and other vehicles, I
felt it necessary to report these defects and unsafe conditions present within the
population of Honda off-road motocross motorcycles in order to protect other children
and adults from being seriously injured or killed by these objectively defective Honda
and Denso products.

It is important these companies and products are now investigated and subsequently
recalled in order to preclude another serious injury or potential death associated with
these unreasonably dangerous and unsafe motorcycles.
VII. THE 2014 HONDA CRF250R INCIDENT OFF-ROAD MOTOCROSS
MOTORCYCLE.
Image 001 was captured during an early non-destructive visual only inspection of the
incident 2014 Honda CRF250R.

The stator is an electrical component located within the motorcycle’s engine behind a
left side metal engine cover. As the engine rotates, magnets are rotated, on a rotor or
flywheel, around a set of copper windings and generate electrical current which then
goes on to provide ignition and spark to the engine in order for the engine to run and
continue running.

If a stator copper wire becomes an open circuit (a wire breaks), the motorcycle’s stator
will no longer output electricity properly. These off-road machines do not have a 12
VDC battery on board designed in. Therefore, if the stator’s electrical output is mechanically interrupted, the engine will almost immediately stop firing and will
suddenly and unexpectedly stop running and shut off, potentially leading to a crash
likely resulting in serious injury or death.
VIII. THE DEFECTIVE HONDA AND DENSO STATOR.
Image 002 is the actual incident Honda motorcycle’s Denso stator assembly minus its
rotor.

The connection of the copper winding is at issue and the wire that fractured and failed
causing a serious motorcycle crash resulting in the operator’s paralysis can be seen
above (and below next page with magnification) partially within its connector surrounded
by solder.
Image 003 is with magnification of the solder ball covering the copper wire and its crimp
connector. Please notice the fracture and disconnect area are located around the
outside diameter (and through the wire) of the copper wire in image 003. Obviously,
this wire should not be in this fractured and disconnected improper condition absent a
product defect.

The fracture and disconnection of this wire caused an open circuit of the electrical circuit
powering the ignition to occur.

When power to the ignition is eliminated the motorcycle’s engine almost immediately
shuts off, blink of an eye fast. We have tested exemplar stators and an exemplar 2014
Honda CRF250R off-road motocross motorcycle and produced video in which we
purposefully interrupted the stator electrical output and measured the time in which ittakes for the engine to suddenly shut off during operation. Loss of engine power can
cause a loss of vehicular control.

When a motorcycle’s engine unexpectedly stops running and unintentionally suddenly
shuts off, a motorcycle may become difficult, if not impossible, to control and may cause
a crash resulting in serious injury or death.

The [REDACTED] Ignition Switch Recalls present similar circumstances to the known
defects regarding Honda and Denso products. Although the parts involved are different
from the [REDACTED] automotive ignition key switch recall from 2014, the results are
very similar in that much as if a [REDACTED] ignition fails and shuts off a motor vehicle’s engine
a crash and serious injury or death can occur, the result of a failed Denso stator in a

Honda off-road motocross motorcycle is the same in that sudden unintended engine
shut off while in motion occurs which can cause a loss of vehicular control, a
subsequent crash and result in serious injury or death to children, the retail consumer or
other rider (other parts involved but same unsafe and unreasonably dangerous
conditions and results).

Additionally, the Honda CRF250R’s engine cannot be restarted after stator and
therefore engine failure occurs. Once the stator failure occurs, the left side of the
engine must be disassembled, a new stator added and engine reassembly, then the
Honda CRF250R can be restarted and ridden.

We are submitting attached herewith a metallurgical report from a co-expert concerning
the metallurgical failure mode of the 2014 Honda CRF250R incident stator.

VIII. THE COVER UP RE WHAT DID HONDA AND DENSO KNOW AND WHEN
CONCERNING THE DEFECT WITHIN THE HONDA CRF250R ENGINE.

It is clear both Honda and Denso knew of the problems and defects associated with
their defective products for years but failed to voluntarily recall their defective products.
Honda had actual knowledge of the product defect for a lengthy period of time and thus
far to date has failed to do the right thing and failed to voluntarily recall their product(s).

Honda’s supplier, Denso, failed to appreciate the potential results of wire failure within
the stator assembly and did not properly understand what would happen if a failure
were to occur.
Concerning Honda’s supplier Denso, we do not know whether the defective
manufacture of motorcycle stators has occurred for other brands and applications and
whether defective stator assemblies have been supplied to other motorcycle
manufacturers.

It is conceivable the defective Denso stator issue is not limited to Honda motorcycles.

It would be important for CPSC to determine whether defective Denso stators are in
other brands of motorcycles, because the product defect may not be limited to Honda
off-road motocross motorcycles and may affect other brands of motorcycles as well.

Honda failed to take responsibility for the defect and blamed others for their product’s
failure. Honda continued to market and sell the Honda CRF250R after and while having
actual knowledge of the product defects present within their engines.

The cover up of the product defect and failure to recall shocks the conscious and
intentionally exposes children, retail end user consumers and other riders to
unreasonable risk of serious injury or death.

Please investigate Honda and Denso regarding this Report and Complaint and the
issues herein, issue stop ride and stop sale orders on all affected model years and
models of Honda off-road motocross motorcycles, pursue recalls and appropriate
remedies for those affected by this unfortunate set of intentional circumstances. Let’s
stop another tragedy before it occurs again. Thank you.

Respectfully submitted.

I believe it was Christmas of 2018, our three children (at time were ages 8,11 and 12) received a "mystery box" as a Christmas gift from a company called Vat19.  The box was marketed to all ages.  In that box were some games, gummy candy and a box of Zen Magnets.  The kids didn't care for many of the items and we either tossed them or put them in a closet to maybe play with later.  Fast forward to Spring of 2020.  My daughter, now 9 almost 10, pulls the Zen Magnets out to play with.  Being almost 10, I figured they were safe for her to play with.  On May 11th, 2020 our daughter got violently ill after dinner.  We thought it was food poisoning from a veggie burger she had eaten as the rest of us had hamburgers and were fine.  Since we were in covid lockdown, we knew she couldn't have a stomach bug.  She got a good night's sleep and was fine for almost 4 days. incident_description:
Re: UNREASONABLE RISK OF SERIOUS INJURY OR DEATH CONCERNING
HONDA CRF250R MULTIPLE YEAR MODELS AND OTHER DISPLACEMENT
MOTOCROSS OFF-ROAD HONDA MOTORCYCLES AND DENSO STATORS
DUE TO ELECTRICAL FAILURE AND SUDDEN UNINTENDED ENGINE SHUT
OFF ENGINE FAILURE DURING OPERATION AND WHILE IN MOTION.

I. REPORT AND COMPLAINT SUBMITTED IN ORDER TO PROTECT
CONSUMERS AND OTHER RIDERS FROM FORESEEABLE FUTHER
INJURIES OR DEATH DUE TO KNOWN UNSAFE AND UNREASONABLY
DANGEROUS HONDA AND DENSO DEFECTIVE PRODUCTS.

This Report and Complaint is respectfully submitted to the United State Consumer
Product Safety Commission in order to prevent foreseeable further injuries and
potential deaths due to known defective products put into the stream of
commerce by Honda and Denso and sold to Americans countrywide and affecting
certain motorcycles worldwide.

II. AMERICAN HONDA MOTOR CO., INC., HONDA MOTOR CO., LTD., DENSO
CORPORATION AND THE HONDA CRF250R.
This Report and Complaint and attachment(s) concerns certain model years Honda
CRF250R motocross off-road motorcycles manufactured by Honda Motor Co., LTD in
Japan and sold in the United States by American Honda Motor Co., Inc., with stators
incorporated thereto manufactured by Denso Corporation.
The population of affected Honda off-road motocross motorcycles are unsafe and
unreasonably dangerous to operate and must now be investigated, recalled and
properly remedied.

III. SUPERIOR COURT OF CALIFORNIA COUNTY OF LOS ANGELES
UNLIMITED CIVIL CASE.

In re and subsequent to the [REDACTED] [settled favorably for the Plaintiff]), we present facts that uncontrovertibly
demonstrate the clear existence of product defects that make certain model year Honda
CRF250R motorcycles unsafe and unreasonably dangerous to operate resulting in
unreasonable risk of serious injury or death.

American Honda Motor Co., Inc., Honda Motor Co., LTD., and Denso Corporation have
known for years about the foregoing product defects but have failed to report or recall
their defective unreasonably dangerous products.

IV. SUDDEN UNINTENDED ENGINE SHUT OFF DUE TO PRODUCT DEFECT.

The product defects contained within the 2014 and many other year model Honda
CRF250Rs, because they can result in the motorcycle’s engine suddenly and
unexpectedly turning off during operation and ceasing operation in its entirety while in
motion (unintended engine shut off), which exposes children, retail end users and other
riders to unreasonable risk of serious injury or death because the motorcycle’s engine
can suddenly and unexpectedly stop running and operation without any indication it is
about to fail.

The failure of the engine to continue running when appropriate may cause loss of
control, leading to motorcycle crashes and therefore significantly raises the risk of
serious injury or death.

V. REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION OF HONDA AND DENSO; REQUEST FOR
INVESTIGATION AND RECALL OF UNREASONABLY DANGEROUS
PRODUCTS.

This Report and Complaint are submitted to formally request investigation of Honda and
Denso and recalls of the affected Honda CRF250R (and Honda CRF450R [and any
other model using similar Denso stators]) off-road motocross motorcycle populations in
the United States in order to reduce the unreasonable risk of serious injury or death to other unsuspecting operators. This Report and Complaint should be forwarded to your
counterparts in Canada and Europe wherein Honda has marketed and sold its defective
CRF250R off-road motocross motorcycles.

This Report and Complaint concerns a 2014 model year Honda CRF250R incident off road motocross motorcycle, a similar brand new 2014 model year Honda CRF250R
exemplar off-road motocross motorcycle, other similar models, and approximately five
or more years-worth of production Honda CRF250R motorcycles.

Multiple model years and multiple displacement off-road motorcycles are affected by the
product defect(s) and should be recalled by the manufacturer.

To our knowledge, Honda and Denso and their various business entities have not
voluntarily recalled these products.

Stator failures have occurred in the United States and Europe. Stator failures have
occurred with racing teams.

The manufacturer has subsequently improperly used or directed to be used, epoxy as a
means to secure defective stator wires. Honda likes gluing together important electrical
connections and Denso does not know whether their stators will be used on
motorcycles with or without 12VDC batteries and the results thereof. Both are
significant failures and embarrassments to Honda and Denso respectively.

The use of epoxy to additionally secure defective stator wires is below the standard of
care and not in accord with industry standards.

Honda and Denso have actual knowledge of the product defects that form the basis of
this Report and Complaint.

Honda and Denso should provide the Consumer Product Safety Commission with all
information, data and documents relevant to the matter in order to facilitate
determination of the scope of the defective stator’s utilization in the population of
motorcycles it has sold to the American public and worldwide. A thorough investigation
by the CPSC will likely uncover the defects are both manufacturing and design defects.

A recall of all affected Honda off-road motorcycles using defective Denso stators will
help ensure no children or adults are seriously injured or killed as a result of Honda’s
knowing and continued use of defective electrical components.
VI. HONDA STATOR FAILURES AND UNINTENDED ENGINE SHUT OFF
RESULTING IN ENGINE FAILURE AND SUBSEQUENT OPERATOR
PARALYSIS.

I was retained in order to look into a 2014 Honda CRF250R off-road motocross
motorcycle, its sudden unintended engine shut off and crash, operated by a licensed
professional rider, during practice, on a motorcycle closed-circuit dirt track.

The facts of the case indicate the incident 2014 Honda CRF250R’s engine suddenly
and unintentionally shut off during normal and foreseeable operation, resulting in a
horrendous crash and subsequent rider paralysis. An objectively tragic outcome directly
caused Honda’s defective product.

As part of the case workup, we determined a copper wire in the motorcycle’s stator
located within the engine of the incident motorcycle had failed, fractured and
disconnected. The stator is made by Denso for Honda is at issue concerning these
defective unreasonably dangerous off-road motocross motorcycles, please see infra.

If a stator copper wire fractures the result is the engine shuts off (extremely fast, no prior
warning) in under 4/10’s of a second. Stators are not generally considered wear items
and are expected to last the life of most motorcycles.

As general mechanical and operational propositions and industry standards, stator
wires do not just become disconnected absent something more. The stator is internal to
the motorcycle’s engine and it is not a component that can be damaged by merely
operating and riding these machines.

The crash of this 2014 Honda CRF250R off-road motocross motorcycle left the operator
seriously injured resulting in paralysis and he is now permanently handicapped in a
wheelchair for the rest of his life due to a particular defective Honda motorcycle.

As a court qualified motorcycle expert in the field of motorcycles and other vehicles, I
felt it necessary to report these defects and unsafe conditions present within the
population of Honda off-road motocross motorcycles in order to protect other children
and adults from being seriously injured or killed by these objectively defective Honda
and Denso products.

It is important these companies and products are now investigated and subsequently
recalled in order to preclude another serious injury or potential death associated with
these unreasonably dangerous and unsafe motorcycles.
VII. THE 2014 HONDA CRF250R INCIDENT OFF-ROAD MOTOCROSS
MOTORCYCLE.
Image 001 was captured during an early non-destructive visual only inspection of the
incident 2014 Honda CRF250R.

The stator is an electrical component located within the motorcycle’s engine behind a
left side metal engine cover. As the engine rotates, magnets are rotated, on a rotor or
flywheel, around a set of copper windings and generate electrical current which then
goes on to provide ignition and spark to the engine in order for the engine to run and
continue running.

If a stator copper wire becomes an open circuit (a wire breaks), the motorcycle’s stator
will no longer output electricity properly. These off-road machines do not have a 12
VDC battery on board designed in. Therefore, if the stator’s electrical output is mechanically interrupted, the engine will almost immediately stop firing and will
suddenly and unexpectedly stop running and shut off, potentially leading to a crash
likely resulting in serious injury or death.
VIII. THE DEFECTIVE HONDA AND DENSO STATOR.
Image 002 is the actual incident Honda motorcycle’s Denso stator assembly minus its
rotor.

The connection of the copper winding is at issue and the wire that fractured and failed
causing a serious motorcycle crash resulting in the operator’s paralysis can be seen
above (and below next page with magnification) partially within its connector surrounded
by solder.
Image 003 is with magnification of the solder ball covering the copper wire and its crimp
connector. Please notice the fracture and disconnect area are located around the
outside diameter (and through the wire) of the copper wire in image 003. Obviously,
this wire should not be in this fractured and disconnected improper condition absent a
product defect.

The fracture and disconnection of this wire caused an open circuit of the electrical circuit
powering the ignition to occur.

When power to the ignition is eliminated the motorcycle’s engine almost immediately
shuts off, blink of an eye fast. We have tested exemplar stators and an exemplar 2014
Honda CRF250R off-road motocross motorcycle and produced video in which we
purposefully interrupted the stator electrical output and measured the time in which ittakes for the engine to suddenly shut off during operation. Loss of engine power can
cause a loss of vehicular control.

When a motorcycle’s engine unexpectedly stops running and unintentionally suddenly
shuts off, a motorcycle may become difficult, if not impossible, to control and may cause
a crash resulting in serious injury or death.

The [REDACTED] Ignition Switch Recalls present similar circumstances to the known
defects regarding Honda and Denso products. Although the parts involved are different
from the [REDACTED] automotive ignition key switch recall from 2014, the results are
very similar in that much as if a [REDACTED] ignition fails and shuts off a motor vehicle’s engine
a crash and serious injury or death can occur, the result of a failed Denso stator in a

Honda off-road motocross motorcycle is the same in that sudden unintended engine
shut off while in motion occurs which can cause a loss of vehicular control, a
subsequent crash and result in serious injury or death to children, the retail consumer or
other rider (other parts involved but same unsafe and unreasonably dangerous
conditions and results).

Additionally, the Honda CRF250R’s engine cannot be restarted after stator and
therefore engine failure occurs. Once the stator failure occurs, the left side of the
engine must be disassembled, a new stator added and engine reassembly, then the
Honda CRF250R can be restarted and ridden.

We are submitting attached herewith a metallurgical report from a co-expert concerning
the metallurgical failure mode of the 2014 Honda CRF250R incident stator.

VIII. THE COVER UP RE WHAT DID HONDA AND DENSO KNOW AND WHEN
CONCERNING THE DEFECT WITHIN THE HONDA CRF250R ENGINE.

It is clear both Honda and Denso knew of the problems and defects associated with
their defective products for years but failed to voluntarily recall their defective products.
Honda had actual knowledge of the product defect for a lengthy period of time and thus
far to date has failed to do the right thing and failed to voluntarily recall their product(s).

Honda’s supplier, Denso, failed to appreciate the potential results of wire failure within
the stator assembly and did not properly understand what would happen if a failure
were to occur.
Concerning Honda’s supplier Denso, we do not know whether the defective
manufacture of motorcycle stators has occurred for other brands and applications and
whether defective stator assemblies have been supplied to other motorcycle
manufacturers.

It is conceivable the defective Denso stator issue is not limited to Honda motorcycles.

It would be important for CPSC to determine whether defective Denso stators are in
other brands of motorcycles, because the product defect may not be limited to Honda
off-road motocross motorcycles and may affect other brands of motorcycles as well.

Honda failed to take responsibility for the defect and blamed others for their product’s
failure. Honda continued to market and sell the Honda CRF250R after and while having
actual knowledge of the product defects present within their engines.

The cover up of the product defect and failure to recall shocks the conscious and
intentionally exposes children, retail end user consumers and other riders to
unreasonable risk of serious injury or death.

Please investigate Honda and Denso regarding this Report and Complaint and the
issues herein, issue stop ride and stop sale orders on all affected model years and
models of Honda off-road motocross motorcycles, pursue recalls and appropriate
remedies for those affected by this unfortunate set of intentional circumstances. Let’s
stop another tragedy before it occurs again. Thank you.

Respectfully submitted.
[REDACTED]

incident_description:
I am a 47 year old mother of two teenage sons, and I have been doing laundry for close to 30 years since being shown by my mother.  For much of that time, I used the old fashioned top load agitator machines, and I was always in the habit of using a full capful of laundry detergent for each large load (I guess it turns out that we have been heavy-handed when adding detergent).

About 8-9 years ago, my husband and I purchased a new [REDACTED] washer without the agitator.  The instruction manual was quite vague, but I didn't think anything of it at the time, and I continued to follow my same laundry routine.

   I didn't think to read the back of the detergent bottles all these years because their overall appearance never changed...I did The laundry as I always had done out of habit, unaware that I was using too much detergent.  The cap sizes never changed, either.  Why are they still so large?  Why are detergents being concentrated (never realized before) without warning customers?  

I became extremely worried a few months ago when I read an article that Tide would be banned in certain states due to presence of carcinogens in its detergent?  What?  I had been using it for years...I thought laundry detergent was safe...it was recommended by [REDACTED] to use in their washers.

It is then that I realized that the default cycle on the [REDACTED] machine I had for the last 8-9 years only did a single 1-2 minute rinse spray.  Even if I hadn't used so much detergent all these years, I still don't know how it could rinse all the clothes properly.  Ironically, all these years, my family and I never noticed.  Our clothes were spun dry so well that I never saw residue, and I think we got used to the strong detergent smell.  Of course, though, as I recently started hand rinsing some of our clothing, I noticed all the detergent built up in the water.

It scares me beyond belief that my sons have been wearing chemically laden clothing since they were little.  My husband has a background in biochemistry and tells me not too worry since my family never had any acute reactions, but I am terrified to hear that laundry detergent could have potential carcinogens.  What if there are long-term health effects from years of wearing clothes with laundry detergent build-up?
 
I have actually reached out to [REDACTED] and Tide about my concerns and waiting to hear back from [REDACTED].  I also wanted to reach out to an organization about this matter because I think laundry detergent use, especially in HE machines needs to be "regulated".  The instructions on bottles and machines are vague.  What exactly defines a large load of laundry?  It's really more about the water amount than the laundry size, isn't it?  Why is it that washing machine manufacturers do not warn customers that they need to use so much less detergent in these high efficiency machines?  Precise instructions and warnings are desperately needed.  There should be clearly labeled warnings and detailed instructions from both the detergent and washer manufacturers on the amount of detergent to use based on the ratio of water per make and model of machine.  There is too much of a discrepancy right now.

I know this may not seem like a big deal,  but I'm sure many consumers are using too much laundry detergent.  It's bad enough to be sending excess detergent down the drain (not to mention the $), but what about potential safety issues?  The date below is an estimation of when I finally became aware of the fact that I was using too much laundry detergent for the past 8-9 years.

I believe that laundry detergent manufacturers should be required to change their bottles and especially cap sizes...they should not be so big because I think it "encourages" consumers to overpour.  The caps also should have clearly labeled measuring marks (horizontal around cap in a different color) so that consumers can actually see them.  Also, HE washers should have warnings on their machines to inform customers to use a minimal amount of detergent (especially for those of us who had been using traditional top-loads).  Furthermore, I think both washer and detergent manufacturers need to provide specific instructions on the dose of detergent to use per amount of water in machine (not just a subjective load size).  There needs to be a particular dilution ratio, and that should be written in the consumer manual of the washer...or better yet, on the machine, in addition to the detergent bottles.  Thank you.
